cloud-fundamentals.r: A company put everything in one availability zone to save money, and a zone problem took the whole product down for an afternoon. Spreading across two zones cost a little more and turned that class of outage into a non-event.
cloud-fundamentals.x: Know the shared responsibility line, what a region and a zone actually isolate, and which services are regional or global. Design for the failure domain you can afford to lose, then verify it.

identity-and-access.r: A long-lived access key was committed to a public repository and abused within minutes to start expensive machines. Roles with short-lived credentials removed the key, and budgets with alerts limited the bill.
identity-and-access.x: Identity is the new perimeter. Use roles, not keys, enforce multi-factor on humans, scope policies to resources and conditions and review unused permissions regularly.

virtual-networks.r: A database was placed in a public subnet 'temporarily' and exposed to the internet. Keeping data in private subnets with access only through the application tier made that mistake harder to make.
virtual-networks.x: Network design is hard to change later. Plan address space, tiers, egress control and private endpoints, and remember that security rules and routes are both needed for a path to work.

compute-and-storage.r: A batch workload ran on always-on machines at full price. Moving it to short-lived instances that could be interrupted, with checkpoints, cut the bill by more than half.
compute-and-storage.x: Match the abstraction to the workload and your team: virtual machines, containers or functions. Understand durability, performance and cost of each storage type and plan for how you will migrate later.

dns-and-cdn.r: A cached error page was served by the CDN for an hour after a brief origin failure. Setting a short cache time for errors and purging on recovery avoided long-lasting damage.
dns-and-cdn.x: A CDN is a distributed cache and a security layer. Set cache rules deliberately, protect the origin, plan for invalidation and use health-checked DNS routing for failover.

serverless.r: A function that processed messages was retried after a timeout and charged customers twice. Making the handler idempotent with a request identifier fixed duplicates.
serverless.x: Serverless shifts operations, not responsibility. Design for retries and duplicates, watch concurrency and downstream limits, know cold start behaviour and keep an eye on cost at scale.

kubernetes-on-cloud.r: Upgrades of the managed cluster were postponed until the version was out of support, and the jump needed several risky steps. Smaller regular upgrades would have been safer.
kubernetes-on-cloud.x: Managed does not mean hands-off. You own node pools, upgrades of workloads and add-ons, identity integration and cost. Plan version support windows and test upgrades first.

monitoring-and-logging.r: A team found out about an outage from customers because their only alarm watched CPU. Alerting on the user-facing error rate and latency would have fired within a minute.
monitoring-and-logging.x: Collect audit logs, metrics and traces centrally, alert on symptoms, and control retention and cost. Protect audit trails from deletion by anyone with normal access.

security-and-governance.r: A developer created a storage bucket open to the public. A guardrail policy at the organisation level now blocks that setting for everyone, so the mistake can no longer reach production.
security-and-governance.x: Preventive guardrails beat detective alerts. Organise accounts so policies apply by default, automate evidence for audits and keep break-glass access tightly controlled and monitored.

managed-services-and-cost.r: A forgotten test environment ran for months and cost more than the production database. Tagging by owner and a weekly report of idle resources found and removed it.
managed-services-and-cost.x: Cost is an engineering metric. Tag everything, set budgets and alerts, review commitments quarterly and weigh managed-service price against the operations work you avoid.

high-availability-and-disaster-recovery.r: A company had a disaster recovery plan on paper, but the first real test found the backups were missing a key table. After regular drills, the next recovery matched the planned time.
high-availability-and-disaster-recovery.x: Define recovery time and recovery point with the business, pick the cheapest design that meets them, and test it. An untested plan is a hypothesis.

landing-zones-and-multi-account-strategy.r: Everything lived in one account, so a mistake in a test project could affect production. Separate accounts for each environment, with shared guardrails, limited each mistake to its own account.
landing-zones-and-multi-account-strategy.x: Accounts are the strongest boundary you have for blast radius, billing and access. Automate account creation with baseline controls, and plan networking and identity before you have many.

object-storage-and-data-lifecycle.r: A deleted file in a bucket without versioning was gone for good. Turning on versioning with a lifecycle rule to expire old versions made accidental deletes recoverable at a modest cost.
object-storage-and-data-lifecycle.x: Storage bills and risks grow quietly. Use versioning and object lock where recovery matters, lifecycle rules for cost, encryption by default and block public access at the account level.

hybrid-connectivity-and-peering.r: Two networks were peered but traffic did not flow because routes and security rules on one side were missing. Peering is a link, not a full path, and both sides need to allow it.
hybrid-connectivity-and-peering.x: Check address overlaps first, remember peering is usually not transitive and plan bandwidth, latency and redundancy for dedicated links. Prefer private endpoints to reduce exposure.

debugging-cloud-outages.r: A deployment failed with a vague error. Checking identity, network path and quotas in that order showed the role lacked a permission, a one-line fix after minutes of focused checking.
debugging-cloud-outages.x: Most cloud failures are permission, network path or quota. Read the audit log for denied calls, check service health pages, and keep a short checklist for the common causes.
